Facebook Twitter Print Email When the rains fail: Preparing for drought in Central America By Beatriz Barral 14 November 2026 Climate and Environment Across Central America’s so-called Dry Corridor, farming families live at the mercy of the rains. In southwestern Honduras, Anastacio Martínez Gómez has spent most of his 73 years learning to work the land. But experience can only take him so far. "When there’s no water, that’s where you run out of ideas,” he says. In his village of Palagua, dry seasons can last five or six months. For years, a failed maize or bean harvest meant searching for work elsewhere. Then, Mr. Martínez volunteered part of his land for a reservoir – opening up new possibilities for his whole community. The Dry Corridor is a drought-prone region stretching across parts of Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua, where more than seven million people do not have guaranteed access to food. Stark choices When crops fail, families face a stark choice: go hungry or migrate. This year, El Niño has made that choice harder. El Niño is a natural climate pattern caused by unusually warm surface waters in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean. It disrupts weather patterns around the world, affecting rainfall and temperatures. The World Meteorological Organization ( WMO ) says the current event could be unprecedented in strength. In Central America, it is increasing the risk of below-average rainfall and drought. Mr. Martínez grew mainly maize and beans, planting two crops a year. If the rains stopped before the plants matured, he could lose everything. “We would plant the first and second crops, and just like that, we were left with no options.” Hetze Tosta de Machado / WFP Honduras WFP staff member inspects Anastacio's Martinez fish pond during a rural aquaculture activity in Honduras. A reservoir changes the equation That began to change when a project was launched to build a large water reservoir in the community. There was one condition: the farmers had to contribute the land. Mr. Martínez volunteered five manzanas ( about 3.5 hectares). “I raised my hand without thinking for even 30 seconds. I said, ‘I’ll give five manzanas for the project’” With support from the World Food Programme ( WFP ), the reservoir and irrigation systems gave farmers a way to store and use water during the dry months. The project also included training to help them grow more types of crops and use water more efficiently. Anastacio and other farmers spent three weeks at Zamorano, the Pan-American Agricultural School in Honduras, learning techniques including how to raise tilapia and grow plantains. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations ( FAO ) also provided agricultural tools. “I was self-taught. All I knew was how to grow maize and beans. Now I can tell you I’m more of a technician,” he says. “I owe all of that to WFP.” His farm is now far more diverse. He grows plantains, cassava, sweet potatoes and malanga, among other crops, and has about 80 mango trees and three fish ponds. He can harvest during both the rainy and dry seasons, and neighbors buy produce directly from the farm. Bountiful crop When his children visit from the United States and Spain, they leave with suitcases full of food. At 73, Mr. Martínez still farms. On Sundays, he rests in a hammock, wearing shorts and a T-shirt, with his dogs beside him. “I sleep peacefully. I have nothing to fear here.” Boris Barrios / PAHO Guatemala Marta Ávalos and neighbours in Camotán, Guatemala, now store grains locally through CERF-supported preparedness measures that strengthen community resilience. In Camotán, Guatemala’s Chiquimula Department, Marta Ávalos is helping her community confront another consequence of drought: the risk of running out of food when crops fail and household incomes disappear. Ms. Ávalos, who grew up in Camotán, knows what it means to struggle for an education. She wanted to be a teacher, but her family could not always afford to keep her in school. She alternated years of study with years of work picking coffee on farms, saving for her school supplies, shoes and backpack. “Families are making the most of what they receive. Before, that mindset didn’t exist,” Ms. Ávalos says. Her mother feared she would come home pregnant rather than with a diploma. It was her grandfather who persuaded her to let her continue. “All right, even if it means eating tortillas with salt, I’ll support you,” her mother told her. “Believe me, I jumped for joy,” Ms. Ávalos recal
